analysis.one_liner: Requires automatic emergency braking on all new large commercial trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in either committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Department of Transportation to write safety rules requiring every new commercial motor vehicle—large trucks and buses—to come equipped with an automatic emergency braking system, which warns the driver of an obstacle ahead and brakes on its own if needed. It also requires that the systems actually be switched on whenever the vehicle is operating. The goal is to prevent rear-end and other collisions involving big trucks.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who shares the road with large trucks and buses: car drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, and the truck drivers themselves. Automatic emergency braking is designed to warn drivers of a vehicle or obstacle ahead and brake automatically if the driver does not respond in time, preventing or softening collisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone sharing the road with large trucks

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Transportation, within one year, to set a federal safety standard requiring automatic emergency braking systems on all new commercial motor vehicles.
Requires the braking system to alert the driver to an obstacle ahead and automatically apply the brakes if needed to avoid or reduce a crash.
Requires a separate federal trucking regulation that the systems actually be used at all times the vehicle is in operation, so the equipment cannot sit switched off.
Requires performance standards for the braking systems, so the technology has to actually work, not just be installed.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and bus operators, who would pay to equip new vehicles with automatic emergency braking systems—costs that could be passed into shipping prices. Safety technology suppliers gain a new market. Owners would bear the cost on new vehicles only, not retrofit the existing fleet.

drawbacks.text: The mandate imposes new equipment costs on motor carriers, and those costs can be passed to customers through shipping prices; the bill text sets a one-year deadline for the rules with no phase-in period specified for compliance beyond the standard's effective date.

Critics of such mandates generally argue automatic emergency braking can produce false alerts or unwanted braking, and that carriers should choose safety technology themselves rather than face a federal requirement—an objection an honest supporter would weigh against the crash-prevention benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad: crashes involving large trucks are among the deadliest on the road, and automatic braking is aimed squarely at the most common type, rear-end collisions. The cost is real but falls on new vehicles only, and the bill includes performance standards rather than an open-ended mandate. On balance a well-targeted safety rule whose costs are modest compared to the harm it targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to two House committees and their subcommittees, and never moved again—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the bill on July 16, 2019, joined by Reps. García of Illinois and Watson Coleman.
Seven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

The bill was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Highways and Transit and Consumer Protection and Commerce subcommittees.
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking operators faced no new equipment mandate from this bill, and the federal safety standard it sought was not enacted during that Congress. Road users did not get the braking requirement it would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking operators; no braking mandate enacted

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require automatic emergency braking on new commercial motor vehicles.

for.name: Reps. Jesús García and Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the record before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote to measure, but all sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats—7 of 231 House Democrats signed on and no Republicans did—so the bill never attracted cross-party support.

industries.note: The bill would require them to equip new trucks with automatic emergency braking, a direct equipment cost. The public benefit—fewer deadly truck crashes—is exactly the cost the industry would bear.
A federal mandate for automatic emergency braking on every new commercial vehicle creates a guaranteed market for the systems they sell.
